title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction: Problem §69: given a prime P, describe the residues of the cubes 1, 2^3, 3^3, ... mod P. Euler's solution: take a primitive root a mod P. Its powers 1, a, a^2, ... run through every nonzero residue class, so each x not divisible by P satisfies x ≡ a^λ for some λ. Then x^3 ≡ a^{3λ}, so the cubic residues are exactly the terms of the progression 1, a^3, a^6, a^9, .... The progression returns to 1 once 3λ is a multiple of P−1. So the number of distinct cubic residues is the least λ with (P−1) | 3λ, namely (P−1)/gcd(3, P−1). Euler then splits primes into the forms 3n+1 and 3n+2. Case I: P = 3n+1, so λ = n. The cubic residues are 1, a^3, ..., a^{3n−3}; there are n of them and 2n non-residues. Case II (continued on p.119): P = 3n+2, so λ = 3n+1 and every nonzero class is a cube. Corollary 2 on the next page adds that for P = 3n+1 each cubic residue arises from exactly three of the cubes 1^3, ..., (3n)^3. In modern terms: the cubing map on the cyclic group (Z/PZ)^* has kernel of size gcd(3, P−1) and image of index gcd(3, P−1). This page applies the paper's general primitive-root method to the case k = 3.
errors: The claim 'every prime is of form 3n+1 or 3n+2' omits P = 3. The case is trivial (every residue mod 3 is a cube), so this is a gap, not an error.
The residue 0 (x divisible by P) is tacitly excluded, which is standard for Euler.

The existence of a primitive root is assumed. Euler's own existence argument in this memoir is generally regarded as incomplete; it was made rigorous by Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae §55), who also credits Legendre's attempt.

ideas.what: Reducing the residues of x^3 mod p to the powers a^{3λ} of a primitive root a
ideas.modern_name: Index (discrete logarithm) method for power residues; image of the k-th power map on a cyclic group
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449, where the term 'radix primitiva' appears); systematised by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), Section III
ideas.where_published: E449 (Novi Commentarii 18, 1774); related earlier work in E262 'Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta'

ideas.what: The number of cubic residues mod p is (p−1)/3 if p ≡ 1 (mod 3), and p−1 (all classes) if p ≡ 2 (mod 3)
ideas.modern_name: Number of k-th power residues = (p−1)/gcd(k, p−1)
ideas.where_published: E449; the general k-th power version appears in Euler's earlier residue papers (E262) and in Gauss's Disquisitiones

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-known application of primitive roots to cubic residues. The result is classical and correctly attributed to Euler and Gauss; nothing on the page is new.
transcription_corrections: The last exponent of the final progression, read as a^{3n−3}, is badly printed in the scan (it could look like a^{3n−1}). Mathematically it must be a^{3n−3}, since the next page says the following term a^{3n} gives unity again.
The next page's transcription 'a^{9n} [?]' is correct: the last term is a^{3(3n)} = a^{9n}.
